text: Some plastics soak up water from the air, and wet pellets make bad parts.
Here's how they get dried.
The desiccant resin dryer.
Pellets sit in a hopper on top of the machine.
Hot, very dry air is blown up through them,
and pulls the moisture out of the pellets over a few hours.
The wet air goes back to the dryer, through a filter and a cooler,
into a bed of desiccant that soaks up the water.
Two beds take turns. One dries the air, while the other is heated to drive its water out.
The result is air with a dew point of minus forty degrees.
But a dryer can quietly stop working.
Dust clogs the filters, so the airflow drops.
A heater or valve fails, and the desiccant stays saturated.
Leaky hoses let wet air in, and a low hopper means the pellets don't stay long enough.
Wet resin gives silver streaks, bubbles and brittle parts.
Warning signs: the dew point rising, splay on the parts, and return air temperature out of its normal range.
So: clean the filters every week.
Watch the dew point, and set the temperature and drying time from the resin datasheet.
Keep the hopper full and the hoses tight, and replace the desiccant on schedule.
Dry resin. Strong parts.
